name: coreml

members.name: UnsupportedOp
members.summary: A traced op has no MIL translation.
members.extended:
Named rather than generic because the alternative failure — emitting
a package that quietly lacks a layer — produces a model that loads
and returns plausible numbers.

members.name: CoreMLModel
members.signature: CoreMLModel(path: str, input_name: str, output_name: str, compute_units: ComputeUnits = ComputeUnits.ALL, precision: str = 'FLOAT32')

methods.name: __init__
methods.signature: __init__(path: str, input_name: str, output_name: str, compute_units: ComputeUnits = ComputeUnits.ALL, precision: str = 'FLOAT32')

methods.name: predict
methods.extended:
The input must be a host tensor: Core ML reads host memory, and
moving a Metal tensor here would hide a copy the caller did not
ask for. Move it explicitly with `.to("cpu")`.

methods.name: verify
methods.summary: Largest absolute difference against the eager model.
methods.extended:
Shapes agreeing is not evidence: a package missing a layer has
the right shape and returns plausible numbers. This runs both and
compares values.

parameters.name: model
parameters.description: The eager model this package was exported from.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Input to run through both. A host tensor.

returns.description:
`max|coreml - eager|`. Expect ~1e-7 for a float32 export
and ~1e-3 relative for float16.

methods.name: compute_plan
methods.summary: Which device Core ML assigns each operation to.
methods.extended:
Requires macOS 14.4+; an empty plan there means *unknown*, not
*unaccelerated*.

methods.name: close
methods.summary: Release the compiled model and the artifacts Core ML cached.

members.summary: A Core ML package written by Lucid, loaded and ready to run.
members.extended:
Holds the `.mlpackage` on disk plus the compiled model Core ML
produced from it. Compilation happens once, when the handle is
created, because it is the expensive step — hundreds of milliseconds
for a real network — and every prediction afterwards reuses it.

members.name: PlacementSummary

methods.name: ane_fraction
methods.summary: Share of computation the Neural Engine takes, 0.0 to 1.0.
methods.extended:
`0.0` on a model asked to use the ANE is the signal that the
request did not take — most often because the program is float32,
which the Neural Engine does not run.

members.summary: Where a model's operations are scheduled.
members.extended:
`const` operations carry no device assignment — they are data, not
computation — so they are counted separately and kept out of the
fraction. Reporting 21% ANE for a model whose every computation runs
on the ANE would be true of the raw operation list and useless.

members.name: ComputeUnits
members.summary: Processors Core ML may schedule the model on.
members.extended:
`CPU_AND_NE` is the reason this package exists: it is the only way
to reach the Neural Engine, which neither of Lucid's own backends
(Accelerate, MLX) targets.

members.name: Precision
members.summary: Weight and activation precision of the exported program.
members.extended:
`FLOAT32` is the default because an export should agree with the
model it came from; Core ML's own default is `FLOAT16`, which the
Neural Engine wants and which costs roughly 1e-4 against the eager
model.

members.name: export
members.signature: export(model: Module, example: Tensor, path: str, precision: Precision = Precision.FLOAT32, compute_units: ComputeUnits = ComputeUnits.ALL, output_field: str | None = None)
members.summary: Trace `model`, write a `.mlpackage` at `path`, and load it.

parameters.name: model
parameters.description:
Must be in `eval()` mode: an exported graph is an inference
graph, and a training-mode dropout is refused rather than
silently turned into an identity.

parameters.name: example
parameters.description:
Supplies the input shape and dtype; its values are irrelevant.
The exported model's input shape is fixed to it.

parameters.name: precision
parameters.description:
Precision of the program body. `FLOAT32` keeps the export
faithful to the model it came from; `FLOAT16` is what the
Neural Engine runs. Inputs and outputs stay float32 either way.

parameters.name: compute_units
parameters.description: Which processors Core ML may schedule on.

parameters.name: output_field
parameters.description:
Attribute to export when the model returns an output dataclass.
`None` takes `logits`, which the zoo's output types carry.

raises.description: The model is in training mode.
The trace contains an operation with no MIL translation.

members.name: load
members.extended:
Feature names are read from the package, so this works on packages
Lucid did not write.

parameters.name: compute_units
parameters.description:
Which processors Core ML may schedule on. Reaching the Neural
Engine also needs the package to be float16 — check with
`CoreMLModel.compute_plan`.

raises.description:
Core ML could not compile or load the package; its own message
names the offending layer.

summary: `lucid.coreml` — export Lucid models to Core ML, and run them on the ANE.
extended:
Lucid computes on Accelerate (CPU) and MLX (Metal).  Neither targets the
Neural Engine, so a whole processor on every machine Lucid supports was
unreachable; the same gap meant a model trained here could not ship inside
an iOS or macOS app.  Core ML is the only public route to either.

**No third-party dependency.**  The package format is written by
`lucid._C.coreml` — the MIL protobuf, the weight blob, the bundle —
and executed through Apple's own CoreML.framework, which stands beside
Accelerate and Metal rather than beside a pip package.  Nothing under
`lucid/` imports anything external (H4).

**Two things worth knowing before trusting an export.**

*The Neural Engine only runs float16.*  A float32 program asked for with
`ComputeUnits.CPU_AND_NE` does not warn, does not error, and runs at CPU
speed — measured: zero of its operations are scheduled on the ANE.  Pass
`Precision.FLOAT16` to actually reach it, and expect the ~1e-4 that
half precision costs.  `CoreMLModel.compute_plan` reports where the
operations really landed, so this is checkable rather than inferred from a
stopwatch.

*Coverage is narrow and loud.*  The mapped operations are the ones real
models were measured to emit; anything else raises
`UnsupportedOp` naming the gap, because a package quietly missing a
layer still loads and still returns plausible numbers.
examples:
import lucid, lucid.coreml as cml

    model = lucid.models.create_model("resnet_18_cls").eval()
    x = lucid.zeros(1, 3, 224, 224)

    cm = cml.export(model, x, "/tmp/r18.mlpackage",
                    precision=cml.Precision.FLOAT16,
                    compute_units=cml.ComputeUnits.CPU_AND_NE)
    cm.verify(model, x)        # max|coreml - eager|
    cm.compute_plan()          # PlacementSummary(ANE=69, CPU=2, ane=97%)
    y = cm.predict(x)
